text: AI agents read email, browse the web and call tools, and they do what the text in front of them says. Hide one line in a web page, and an agent will hand over your keys. Asking the model nicely does not fix that.
Tripline does not trust the model. It follows every piece of data, and decides what the agent may do with it. Here, a stolen key is stopped at the wire, while a legitimate message passes.
Here is the attack, replayed. Without Tripline, a poisoned message makes the agent mail out cloud keys. With Tripline, the send is blocked, and the user's task still completes.

But a scripted agent proves little. This is a real Gemini model, a real poisoned page and real network sockets. The model fetches the page, follows the hidden instruction, reads the secret file, and posts it to the attacker. Then it gives the user a perfectly normal summary. Behind Tripline, the same model makes the same attempt, and the call is refused. Whenever the model took the bait, the secret leaked without Tripline, and never behind it.
Before any of this, the scanner inspects tool manifests. A poisoned tool is blocked with evidence, and a hash lockfile catches a rug pull, where a server quietly edits a tool after you approved it.

Now try to beat it yourself. In the arena you are the attacker: write any message that sneaks the secret out. The X-ray shows where Tripline sees it hiding, even inside base64 or ROT13. One disguise, code words, does get through in a clean session, and we show that openly. With untrusted content around, rule R2 holds it.
Every decision is written to a hash chained flight recorder, with digests instead of secrets. Edit a decision, delete an entry or swap two, and the verifier catches it at exactly that entry.
Tripline is open source and runs entirely in your browser. One command wraps your real MCP config behind it, with a backup and an undo. Tripline. Do not trust the text. Trust the wire.
